content:
Hello,

I am new to Lean, but have been learning and using TLA+ for many years now.

I would like to ask for feedback on a little project, where my goal was to translate a TLA+ spec into a high-level Lean "spec", and then write a lower-level Lean "implementation", and then verify that the latter implements the former.

What I appreciate about TLA+ is that I can use it to describe only the concurrent aspect of a program, and then mentally map it to actual code. So I am interested in doing something similar with Lean, by splitting a program into two parts(spec + implementation), where the additional benefit is the verification.

Also, I speculate that with AI, one could then not pay too much attention to the lower-level implementation part, as long as the fact that it implemented the spec part had been verified.

The TLA+ spec, and the Lean version, are both at https://github.com/gterzian/lean_concurrency

TLA+ spec, Lean spec, and Lean implementation.

I also wrote about the experience in https://medium.com/@polyglot_factotum/on-what-the-future-of-software-looks-like-today-ea9d53e647a7

Incidentally, this exercise also surfaced a bug in my original TLA+ spec.

Please let me know what you think.

I encourage you to check the project called Loom from Verselab. It is a framework that allows you to embed monadic DSLs using Dijkstra monads. But the relevant part is that one of their languages Veil is built on it which resembles Ivy

I agree with Shreyas - have a look into Veil. What I'd like to see is how (in an idiomatic way) one can map TLA+ into Veil, and where this is perhaps is not possible.

BTW, Veil has its own channel!
Thanks for the info, both Loom and Veil look interesting and an upgrade from my manual attempts.

So I have looked both at Loom and Veil.

What Loom does is beyond my understanding for now; for Veil I can follow along the examples but it feels far to abstract for me.

I'm not looking for a DSL, I want to be able to write the actual inductive stuff, much more like what Diehl is doing when modelling the Caverna game. I find that to be much closer to the abtraction level of TLA+, which is what I am looking for.

But then what I am looking to do in addition, is the equivalent of implementing the Caverna game in Lean, and then proving that the implementation refines the spec, where the spec would be like the Lean code in Diehl's blog.

(note that my project is not the actual Caverna game, I am just using it to tie it to the example of Diehl's blog)

So I understand that something like Veil could make the proving part easier, but I just want something that reads more like normal math defining a TLS.
Loom is a framework in which you can write Veil
In fact I think this is Veil 2.0
So it makes sense that Loom is not directly what you want. You want veil written on top of loom

@Artur Lojewski

What I'd like to see is how (in an idiomatic way) one can map TLA+ into Veil, and where this is perhaps is not possible.

This should always be possible. In fact, one of our goals for this year is to make it much, much easier to port specifications from TLA+ into Veil. This is quite preliminary at this stage (we haven't added good syntactic conventions to Veil to support it), but we have translated a few specifications from TLA+, including MultiPaxos: https://github.com/verse-lab/veil/tree/veil-2.0-preview/Examples/TLA

Part of this effort is that Veil 2.0 (currently in preview) includes a verified TLC-style model checker, with performance quite comparable to TLC.

Once we clean up the user experience for some TLA-like abstractions (mainly sets and cardinalities), we'll document all of this so it's more accessible to users. We're aware the documentation is very lacking at the moment.

Gregory Terzian said:

I'm not looking for a DSL, I want to be able to write the actual inductive stuff, much more like what Diehl is doing when modelling the Caverna game.

Just to clarify a bit: Veil does have a DSL ("frontend"), which defines all the inductive stuff you'd write manually, but there is a lot more than the DSL ("backend"): explicit state (TLC-style) and symbolic model checking (Apalache-style), integration with SMT solvers so you see concrete counterexamples to induction, etc.

Integrating more tightly with normal Lean developments has been on our radar for a while, along two dimensions:

  1. writing a "pure" Lean frontend to all the Veil backend tools
  2. exporting clean definitions from the Veil DSL, such that users can more easily prove things like refinement wrt. regular Lean specifications

We've had other things on our plate recently, but we are planning to work on refinement later this year, so we'll naturally tackle these points. I'd be keen to hear what kind of features / interaction patterns would make your life easier.

I've encoded your spec in Veil using Claude, by the way. You can try it here at try.veil.dev, if you'd like to take a look.

@George Pîrlea Thank you for your response and for the spec translation.

So I have used TLA+ for about 6 years now, although never with a proof and relying on the model checker only. And of-course I have had to answer the question: "what is the point of TLA+ if it isn't tied to the code" quite often during that time.

So what attracted me to Lean, like two weeks ago, was the idea that I could do both the kind of design work I do in TLA+, and then tie it to an actual Lean implementation, perhaps one calling into another language using FFI.

So right now my focus is on getting familiar with Lean, and so while I can imagine Veil could help me automate the verification part and also offer me a higher-level syntax, it also feels like yet another "language" to learn, and I am struggling with Lean enough as it is. I also quite like to see how Lean can be used to implement a kind of TLA+ by hand.

Also, while I can imagine that Veil makes you life easier with proofs using #check_invariants, especially in more complicated systems, so far I just had the AI write all the Lean, while I focus only on making sure the theorem is what I have in mind.

So that's just a bit of backstory, and also an explanation for why for now I think I will stick to basic Lean.

I am also a maintainer of the Servo web engine, and find that some of the most difficult bugs to fix are intermittent test failures related to broken concurrent algorithms.

So I have this rough idea of implementing a web engine in a combo of Lean and Rust(via FFI), where the Lean part would consists of a kind of TLS for all the concurrent state in the engine, and then there would be a Lean implemenation, probably using channels and threads or tasks, which would implement the TLS, and then it would call into Rust for purely sequential algorithms.

I'm thinking of doing this in layers, where initially the Rust code would still do some threading, and where the threading would move to the Lean layer over time, where the goal is for the Rust to be only sequential (because sequential code seems less in need of formal verification, although there you can also think of things like proving certain memory limits and what not).

So what I need is really:

  1. A Lean TLS (probably more than one, there would be one global TLS for the engine as a whole, and one TLS per sub-component).
  2. A lean (probably channel-based) implementation of the TLS (some sub-TLS could use mutex/condvar).
  3. A refinement proof for 2 -> 1
  4. FFI to call into Rust (unverified but sequential only)
For rust code in Lean you have Aeneasand project peregrine

@Gregory Terzian Very interesting to hear. All the best!

We had an undergraduate a while ago do something similar using the Lean/Rust FFI & implementing a version of Raft, with the core logic in Lean and the networking code in Rust. We didn't get to the stage where we wrote any significant proofs, but it might still be useful for you to look at: https://github.com/filbertphang/bythors/tree/raft-only
